svg.text: THE BILL — days to fit a scene, half a minute for every frame after

a.data-tip: Between 100 thousand and 300 thousand optimisation iterations, about one to two days on a single NVIDIA V100, for one scene. Each iteration renders 4096 rays with a coarse and a fine network. Adam, learning rate decaying exponentially over the run.

g.data-tip: One to two days of continuous optimisation on a single V100, for a single scene, before you can render anything at all.
g.text: 100k to 300k iterations, 1 to 2 days, one V100

a.text: Both numbers from Sec. 5.3. Each iteration: 4096 rays, coarse and fine.
NV and SRN, the other per-scene methods, also take at least
12 hours a scene; only LLFF, pretrained once, skips the fit.
Output: about 5 MB of weights, roughly 3000 times
smaller than the over 15 GB of grids LLFF stores per scene.

a.data-tiphead: Render cost, and where it comes from
a.data-tip: Every pixel needs its own ray, and every ray needs 64 coarse queries plus 192 fine ones. At 800 by 800 that is 640 thousand rays for one frame. The paper reports between 150 and 200 million network queries per rendered image, taking about 30 seconds per frame on a V100. That figure lives in the supplementary implementation details, not the main body.

g.data-tip: One ray per pixel. An 800 by 800 render needs 640 thousand of them; the real scenes need 762 thousand.
Sixty-four evaluations of the coarse network plus 192 of the fine network: 256 forward passes for a single pixel.
Between 150 and 200 million network evaluations for one rendered image, which is what the wall-clock number reduces to.

a.text: about 30 seconds per frame on a V100
Roughly 0.03 frames per second. A 10-second clip at 30 fps
is about two and a half hours of rendering.
Provenance: this figure is in the supplement, not Sec. 6.

a.data-tip: The paper frames the comparison as time against space. LLFF processes a small dataset in under ten minutes but produces a voxel grid per input image, over 15 GB for one realistic synthetic scene. NeRF spends days up front and stores about 5 MB, which is less than its own input photographs.
a.text: The paper frames it as time versus space, and wins on space
LLFF: under 10 minutes to process a scene, then over 15 GB of grids for one realistic synthetic scene.
NeRF: one to two days, then about 5 MB — less memory than the input images for a single scene from any of its datasets.
What that framing quietly leaves out is the third axis: what it costs to look at the result, every time you look.

svg.text: Why this number, not the training time, is the one that mattered historically
Training days are paid once per scene and can be left running overnight. Half a minute per frame is paid on every view,
forever, which rules out anything interactive — and view synthesis is judged by moving the camera.
The entire acceleration literature that followed NeRF is aimed at this one line of the paper.
